before: A conventional xenograft implants viable tumour material into a host; an epithelial organoid grows selected cells in supplied matrix and medium; a fragment or slice retains a cut piece of local tissue. Ladan used 300 micrometre (0.3 millimetre) breast slices. None supplies complete human drug metabolism, healthy-organ toxicity or recruitment of new immune cells from human circulation, and every preparation can fail. Fixed archival tissue cannot supply the living input. Whether frozen material is usable must be shown for the particular protocol; Ladan's assay used fresh tissue.

Throughput and repetition depend on how material can be expanded. A xenograft can be passaged into further mice, but each drug comparison needs suitable animals and controls. An established organoid line can be expanded and passaged to compare a drug panel; Sachs reported retention of many source features during extended passaging, not unlimited fidelity. A cut piece has a finite culture window and a limited number of matched conditions; it cannot simply be expanded while retaining the same original neighbourhood. Ladan's group described viability for up to a week. These are practical preparation contrasts, not a universal numerical throughput ranking or an assumption that every organoid survives freezing. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2017.11.010 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10542784/

The useful trade-off is preserved biology against time and repeatability. A characterised PDX supports growth under whole-animal dosing, usually on a months-long establishment clock. Expanded organoids support repeated direct tumour-cell experiments and panels, often over weeks; conventional epithelial cultures usually lack immune cells, while Neal's specialised method retained them. A short-term fragment may preserve resident neighbours for a local-interaction question over days, but their function must be demonstrated. No preparation is universally more predictive because it is more complex. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2018.11.021 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4167608/

The clocks and take rates below belong to different studies. Hidalgo's review described four to eight months to a study-ready PDX. Izumchenko reported 578/1,163 establishment and mean 16 weeks from engraftment to drug exposure, with tumour-type variation: 85 percent in colorectal specimens and 30 percent in breast specimens in that series. Cartry reported a 61.5 percent core-biopsy take rate and six-week median, range four to ten weeks, to a 25-drug colorectal organoid panel. Boileve reported 54/87 establishment (62 percent) and mean 6.8 weeks to a pancreatic chemogram. Ladan used three-day exposures and stated that results can be known in seven to fourteen days; this is a planned window, not an observed turnaround distribution. There were 23/30 usable tests from tumour-containing biopsies. The PDX paper reports 49 percent for 578/1,163; direct count arithmetic is approximately 49.7 percent.

Ladan's breast-slice pilot found 15/20 category matches (75 percent; reported confidence interval 53 to 89 percent), against a pre-set target of at least 55 percent, between the ex vivo anthracycline assay and MRI response after four courses of anthracycline-containing treatment. Both systems used sensitive, intermediate and resistant categories, and neither observed a resistant tumour. Of five disagreements, three were ex vivo sensitive with intermediate MRI response and two the reverse. Among the 23 successful laboratory tests, six were sensitive and 17 intermediate; among the 20 MRI comparisons, four were sensitive and 16 intermediate. This leaves resistance detection untested rather than established. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10542784/

Other agreement measures answer different questions. Vlachogiannis reported 88 percent positive and 100 percent negative predictive values in 21 drug-response comparisons in heavily pretreated gastrointestinal cancers. Boileve reported 83.3 percent sensitivity and 92.9 percent specificity in 34 evaluable pretreated pancreatic patients. Izumchenko compared 129 treatments across 92 patients: 112/129 agreement grouped stable disease with partial and complete responses, while exact-category agreement was 91/129. These endpoints and selected denominators cannot be ranked as head-to-head accuracy or taken as proof that model-guided care improves survival.

Voabil's primary abstract reports that immune-cell reactivation after ex vivo PD-1 blockade in patient-derived tumour fragments predicted clinical response in that study, with perturbation analyses identifying tumour-resident T cells as a key component. This supports a scoped fragment/immune-interaction example, not evidence that choosing treatment from a fragment test improves outcomes. A near-term decision may rule out establishing a new conventional PDX, but does not guarantee a usable fragment; immune presence, movement, recognition and killing remain distinct measurements. Source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-021-01398-3

Dijkstra's colorectal and lung organoid study used master and working biobanks, cryopreserved cultures and experiments below passage 30. That demonstrates a specified bank-and-recovery workflow for those established organoid cultures. It does not show that every organoid line or fresh tumour fragment can be frozen, recovered and retested with unchanged properties. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6558289/

In a wholly fictional development project, D0 supplies one verified malignant preparation. Drug A asks about a direct repair perturbation: a tumour-only organoid supplies a viable-cell count after 48 hours, with division and death measured separately. The invented exposure series is 0.1, 0.3 and 1 micromoles per litre with three wells per condition and vehicle, positive and mechanism controls. Antibody B instead needs compatible tumour and immune populations over a stipulated seven days, with tumour-only, immune-only, matched antibody or carrier, and recognition controls. B's concentration and schedule are missing. The conventional graft's mouse exposure, schedule, assessment day and controls are also missing, so it remains an incomplete proposal. These conditions are not doses established as safe or achievable in people.

A separate fictional three-week decision exercise names real drugs but invents every result. A tumour-only organoid can test a direct olaparib response using an attributed living-cell count after five days; it cannot supply the T cells needed for the pembrolizumab question. Fresh fragments retaining functional resident T cells or a characterised compatible co-culture can address a two-day activation question, with attributed tumour-cell death and recognition controls still needed. A conventional graft cannot restore an intact human immune system and its establishment may miss the deadline. Predicting RNA after BRCA1 loss is a computational hypothesis, not a performed drug exposure. Confirm the actual assay clock: a colorectal six-week median does not forecast the timing for this fictional breast specimen. No choice supplies complete human metabolism, healthy-organ toxicity or every original tumour population.

before: Reading guide (OnCo inference). The task defines what an output means: filling a missing RNA value from an image, estimating a drug response and predicting a gene-disruption response are different tasks, and success at one does not validate another. A virtual perturbation changes a model input and calculates an output; it is not a performed experiment, and masking a gene value is not the same as removing the gene's function. Predicted RNA is not measured RNA, protein activity or patient benefit. Agreement summarised across all genes can conceal poor prediction of the few genes that changed, so compare against simple baselines on the genes that moved. An association learned from untreated tissue does not by itself identify a causal drug effect. Whether a model's output supports treatment selection needs separate intended-use clinical evidence, whereas prioritising experiments is a lesser claim.

Fictional worked example. A model accurately fills missing RNA values from images of familiar samples. That is measurement completion; it says nothing about a drug that was never tested. To claim a drug response, define the intervention and outcome, reserve independent measured experiments, and compare with baselines and the measured response.

Fictional worked example. A model learns RNA responses to interventions in one cell line and correctly predicts additional cells exposed to a familiar intervention. That did not test a never-tested intervention in breast tumour cells; a reserved set of measured interventions and compatible breast-cell data would support a closer evaluation.

Model card in words (a reading guide). Input and tissue cost: the measured data, preprocessing and missing inputs; computation uses data, while new data collection may consume tissue. Output: the predicted object with units, intervention, dose and time. Version and scope: model version, training population and intended task. Evaluation: what was held out, the baselines, error measures and external data. Failure modes: leakage, incompatible inputs, context shift or the wrong endpoint. Cannot establish alone: a performed perturbation, complete cell biology or better clinical outcomes.

Figure reading (fictional teaching scene, light and dark renders agree): panel 1 fills a missing observation, where images paired with RNA from a defined population train a model that outputs a computed RNA value for a held-out donor and is tested against the masked measured value; panel 2 trains on measured responses to familiar X and forecasts withheld Y, tested later against a reserved measured response; panel 3 says a new donor tests donor generalisation, a new intervention tests intervention transfer, and neither automatically tests a new cell type. Computed is not measured, and the population, task and version stay attached.

The original model-choice exercise stipulates a fictional virtual-C-v1 model: compatible measured expression data go in, and normalised RNA expression 48 hours after gene C disruption is predicted. No physical drug exposure occurred. Compare unperturbed or no-change baselines with independently measured responses in reserved new donors and the withheld C intervention. All fitting, threshold and preprocessing choices belong to development. A new donor tests a different transfer question from a new perturbation, cell type or laboratory. This computational result can prioritise a measured experiment; it supplies neither protein effects, immune interactions, safe delivery nor clinical benefit.

before: Preparation and assay card. Input: suitable viable tissue with donor/site/time, collection and transport conditions, dimensions and culture window. Cutting, quality checks and endpoints consume finite material and limit available conditions. Compare baseline quality and untreated or carrier controls with defined exposures. Attribute counts, stain fractions, movement or metabolic signal to the relevant cells, with units, time and denominator. Thresholds are method-specific rather than a universal fragment score. Fragment names the preparation; a drug screen names an experiment it may support. Different pieces from one tumour can contain different populations, so matched treatments still need composition checks.

Primary preparation example. Ladan used 300 micrometre slices and three-day exposure in a defined anthracycline-based assay, measuring morphology, proliferation and apoptosis. Diffusion into slices differs from vascular delivery; host metabolic activation, clearance, organ toxicity and new immune recruitment were not recreated. Preparation injury, poor viability, uneven diffusion, changing populations and non-tumour signal can invalidate interpretation. A failed culture is not evidence of clinical resistance. Contamination is another reason for assay failure; short-term response does not establish durable elimination, systemic safety or benefit.

Endpoint and validation example. Ladan reported 23 usable assays among 30 tumour-containing biopsies; three of the 23 did not proceed to the clinical treatment comparison, leaving 20 evaluable patients and 15 concordant MRI comparisons. The agreement compared sensitive, intermediate and resistant categories after four courses of anthracycline-containing chemotherapy; it is not a binary drug-killing rate. The study did not observe an ex vivo resistant group, limiting assessment of resistance detection. Those denominators, assay version and preoperative setting cannot validate another postoperative choice. Salmon measured matrix-associated T-cell location and movement in viable lung-tumour slices, not treatment-selection benefit.

Fictional reading exercise. Two fragments with different starting malignant-cell fractions both lose total metabolic signal. Equal tumour killing has not been shown. Verify composition and an attributed death endpoint against controls. Retained neighbours can be useful for an immune question only when their viability and relevant function are demonstrated.

Ladan's real study began with 41 consenting people: three did not undergo biopsy and eight biopsies lacked tumour cells, leaving 30 adequate tumour biopsies. Six assays failed the prespecified baseline-apoptosis criterion and one was lost to infection. Of 23 usable results, three people did not receive the chemotherapy, leaving 20 clinical comparisons. The main-text counts are used here; Table 2's footnote instead mentions two people not receiving chemotherapy. The reported interval for 15/20 agreement was 53 to 89 percent, and the pilot's prespecified target was at least 55 percent. Reaching that target supports further investigation, not a demonstration that using the assay to choose care improves outcomes.

The reported breast-study totals imply two sensitive dish calls with sensitive MRI, three sensitive dish calls with intermediate MRI, two intermediate dish calls with sensitive MRI and thirteen intermediate calls matching MRI. Thus 15/20 agree, including thirteen matches in the common intermediate category. Two of four MRI-sensitive tumours were called sensitive in the dish (50 percent), and two of five sensitive dish calls matched MRI sensitivity (40 percent). These are stated comparisons with an imperfect MRI outcome, not validated sensitivity or positive predictive value against known truth. FDA's March 2007 diagnostic-test guidance distinguishes agreement from accuracy when the comparator is not a reference standard. The study's sensitive category required more than 50 percent size reduction after four chemotherapy courses; it is not simply the standard RECIST partial-response category. Usable coverage is 23/30, about 77 percent; a matching clinical comparison was available for 15/30, or 50 percent, including failures and the untreated people in that denominator. Neither ratio measures postoperative benefit.

before: Patient-derived organoids can provide expandable material for repeated experiments when establishment succeeds. They are one part of the broader organoid family. The organoid definition holds the shared construction, consumption, quality-control and readout explanation; the technology record concerns their use as a research resource. A successful culture still needs malignant-cell identity and intended-use checks. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2017.11.010 ; https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2018.11.021

Colorectal cancer: Bertotti and colleagues used xenografts from 85 metastatic colorectal cancer samples and found HER2 amplification in a subset of cetuximab-resistant cases (2011). The abstract describes xenografts, not organoids, and does not establish priority before every clinical trial. Calon and colleagues reported that TGF-beta signalling inhibitors blocked cancer-microenvironment cross-talk and halted disease progression in patient-derived organoid and xenograft experiments (2015). Sources: https://doi.org/10.1158/2159-8290.CD-11-0109 ; https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.3225

Drug-specific agreement can fail to transfer even within colorectal cancer. Ooft and colleagues reported that organoids predicted the biopsied lesion's response in more than 80 percent of people receiving irinotecan-based treatment, but failed to predict response to fluorouracil plus oxaliplatin. The Netherlands Cancer Institute's 2019 research announcement describes 61 patients in the clinical study; Wensink's later review tabulates 29 people in the response-comparison cohort, including ten receiving irinotecan and twelve receiving an irinotecan doublet. Those cohort and regimen denominators are not interchangeable. This was a prediction comparison, not evidence that assigning treatment by the test improved patient outcomes.

Wensink's 2021 review included seventeen publications, five about colorectal cancer; seven used metastatic populations. Its pooled sensitivity was 81 percent and specificity 74 percent for the included response comparisons. The authors warned that these estimates were likely high because some studies lacked quantitative results needed for pooling and not all used a predefined index test; publication or outcome-reporting bias could not be excluded. The pooled establishment estimate was 68.0 percent at patient level and 68.5 percent at sample level, with heterogeneous studies and wide intervals. These are different quantities from response agreement and from clinical utility. The review also reports a 34-day median just to establish organoids from breast biopsies, distinct from a completed drug panel or an individual decision deadline.

Vlachogiannis and colleagues studied organoids from heavily pretreated metastatic colorectal and gastroesophageal cancers. They grew organoids from 70 percent of adequately cellular biopsies and compared model and clinical drug responses in 21 comparisons. The reported sensitivity was 100 percent, specificity 93 percent, positive predictive value 88 percent and negative predictive value 100 percent for those comparisons. These are the study's response metrics with its defined comparators and selected denominator, not 88 percent accuracy for all patients or evidence for a postoperative breast decision. Culture success, response agreement and benefit from assigning treatment remain separate questions.

Boileve and colleagues prospectively enrolled 87 people with pretreated advanced pancreatic cancer, generated 54 organoids (62 percent) and had 34 evaluable patients with clinical follow-up. The 34 evaluable people are about 39 percent of the original 87, not 39 percent of successful cultures. Mean time to a chemogram was 6.8 weeks; reported sensitivity was 83.3 percent and specificity 92.9 percent. Those selected results and routine-care hit versus nonhit comparisons do not establish a randomised treatment-selection benefit or validate a breast-cancer assay.

Colorectal cancer: Bertotti and colleagues used xenografts from 85 metastatic colorectal cancer samples and found HER2 amplification in a subset of cetuximab-resistant cases (2011). The abstract describes xenografts, not organoids, and does not establish priority before every clinical trial. Calon and colleagues reported that TGF-beta signalling inhibitors blocked cancer-microenvironment cross-talk and halted disease progression in patient-derived organoid and xenograft experiments (2015). Sources: https://doi.org/10.1158/2159-8290.CD-11-0109 ; https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.3225

before: Specimen and assay card. Record donor/site/time, living preparation, transport and processing, initial composition, culture history, assay version, concentrations, exposure duration, replicates and control range. Fixed tissue cannot supply living cells; whether previously frozen material can supply the required viable preparation must be demonstrated for that protocol. Input suitability and recovery must be demonstrated for the method. Testing and endpoint processing use finite material. Output needs units, denominator, normalisation and uncertainty; acceptance criteria must be defined for the actual method. Name whether the preparation is dissociated cells, a fresh fragment or an expanded organoid. Mixed samples include normal neighbours, and expansion can change the represented populations.

Handling evidence is method-specific. Ladan and colleagues collected breast tissue in their specified medium, cut 300 micrometre slices and assessed morphology, proliferation and apoptosis after three-day exposure. This is not a general transport or storage protocol for all screens. Growth-rate methods show why baseline counts and control division affect interpretation. Retain failures and exclusions; failed preparation is not clinical resistance. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10542784/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4887336/ Medium, drug access and exposure duration can change the result. Mechanism-relevant controls test whether the claimed interaction can occur; absent required cells or unrealistic exposures can make an experiment uninformative even when a numerical response is available. A laboratory concentration is not a safe human dose.

Fictional example. A well has half the metabolic signal but the same identified viable tumour-cell endpoint count as control. This establishes a changed proxy, not half the cells killed; endpoint equality also does not reconstruct every division and death. Separate death, target engagement, safe human dosing and clinical benefit remain questions. This is an arithmetic and interpretation exercise, not observed patient data. Possible readouts include cell number, metabolism, mass, growth and death. Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is a cellular energy molecule measured by some luminescence assays. Promega's primary assay guidance states that cellular ATP content varies with cell type and physiology and can alter the relation between cell number and light output. A lower ATP signal can therefore reflect fewer cells or a per-cell change, rather than a counted death fraction. Source: https://www.promega.com/-/media/files/resources/protocols/technical-bulletins/0/celltiter-glo-luminescent-cell-viability-assay-protocol.pdf

Restivo and colleagues generated organoids from matched fresh and slow-frozen colorectal tumour tissue from two patients with stage IV disease. Their specified slow-freezing protocol used a cryoprotectant to preserve living material, and the frozen-derived cultures took longer to form than the fresh-derived cultures. This is evidence of recovery under that protocol, not equivalence of all fresh, snap-frozen and viable-cryopreserved samples or a guaranteed turnaround. The handling history, recovery, malignant identity and assay quality need checking for the intended experiment. Preserved molecular material alone does not establish a recoverable living model. Source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-022-04025-0

Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10542784/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4887336/ Medium, drug access and exposure duration can change the result. Mechanism-relevant controls test whether the claimed interaction can occur; absent required cells or unrealistic exposures can make an experiment uninformative even when a numerical response is available. A laboratory concentration is not a safe human dose.

Fictional example. A well has half the metabolic signal but the same identified viable tumour-cell endpoint count as control. This establishes a changed proxy, not half the cells killed; endpoint equality also does not reconstruct every division and death. Separate death, target engagement, safe human dosing and clinical benefit remain questions. This is an arithmetic and interpretation exercise, not observed patient data. Possible readouts include cell number, metabolism, mass, growth and death. Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is a cellular energy molecule measured by some luminescence assays. Promega's primary assay guidance states that cellular ATP content varies with cell type and physiology and can alter the relation between cell number and light output. A lower ATP signal can therefore reflect fewer cells or a per-cell change, rather than a counted death fraction. Source: https://www.promega.com/-/media/files/resources/protocols/technical-bulletins/0/celltiter-glo-luminescent-cell-viability-assay-protocol.pdf

Restivo and colleagues generated organoids from matched fresh and slow-frozen colorectal tumour tissue from two patients with stage IV disease. Their specified slow-freezing protocol used a cryoprotectant to preserve living material, and the frozen-derived cultures took longer to form than the fresh-derived cultures. This is evidence of recovery under that protocol, not equivalence of all fresh, snap-frozen and viable-cryopreserved samples or a guaranteed turnaround. The handling history, recovery, malignant identity and assay quality need checking for the intended experiment. Preserved molecular material alone does not establish a recoverable living model. Source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-022-04025-0

Read a model study as a sequence of explicitly defined groups: people or specimens offered or submitted, preparations yielding a usable model, results compared with a clinical outcome, and results agreeing under the stated rule. Eligibility exclusions, absent tumour, laboratory failures, missing outcomes and people not receiving the treatment belong to different steps. State whether the unit is a person, specimen or treatment comparison; one person can contribute more than one. A percentage among compared cases cannot describe everyone originally offered testing, and an analysis exclusion is not automatically a failed culture. Keep the drug, cancer, treatment history, outcome, clock and assay version attached rather than ranking different studies as competing accuracy scores.

The prospective single-arm SENSOR study enrolled 61 people with metastatic colorectal cancer: 54 were eligible, 31 organoids were generated, 25 cultures were screened against eight drugs and nineteen showed a substantial laboratory response. Six people received an organoid-selected treatment, three vistusertib and three capivasertib, with no objective clinical responses. That observation concerns this panel and selected population; it neither establishes benefit from using the assay nor proves that every organoid method is ineffective. Guillen and colleagues' breast-model report describes a complete response in one person with metastatic triple-negative disease after a model-nominated treatment. That case demonstrates feasibility, without a comparison estimating how often the strategy helps.

Randomised outcome evidence must be assessed for the named assay and use rather than declared absent for all functional testing in solid tumours. Ranjan and colleagues reported a 2023 trial of ChemoID selection versus physician choice from the same chemotherapy list in 78 people with recurrent glioblastoma under the 2016 WHO definition. Enrolment stopped after a prespecified efficacy analysis; the intention-to-treat report gave median overall survival of twelve versus 7.5 months. Participants could provide viable tumour through surgery or biopsy, so the findings do not include every patient with recurrent glioblastoma. Cordgenics supported the assay resources, and two authors declared licensed intellectual-property interests. This is evidence for the studied strategy and population, without validating another assay, organoid system, postoperative breast decision or universal treatment rule.

before: Assay-report axes. Name the malignant population and comparator cells, live input and consumption, drug concentration and exposure, readout and denominator, control range, failures and assay version. A mixed malignant/normal ratio can change through either population; it is not by itself a counted malignant-cell death fraction. Negative or failed experiments do not automatically nominate another clinical treatment. These are reading rules, not changes to the EXALT trial result. Source for growth/readout boundary: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4887336/

The prospective EXALT study tested an image-based single-cell selection approach in 143 people with advanced aggressive blood cancers. Fifty-six were treated according to the assay; 30 of those 56 (54 percent) had progression-free survival more than 1.3 times that on their own previous therapy. The comparator was each person's prior therapy in a single-arm study, not randomised standard care. This result does not show that all tested patients benefited or validate another assay or disease setting. Source: https://doi.org/10.1158/2159-8290.CD-21-0538

EXALT used viable material from blood, bone marrow or lymph nodes. These are method- and disease-specific inputs, not evidence that every blood cancer is easy to sample or that its test transfers to a solid-tumour preparation. The 143 enrolled and tested people, 56 receiving assay-guided therapy and 30 meeting the PFS-ratio endpoint remain distinct groups. The comparator for that endpoint was each person's previous therapy; another twenty people formed a physician-choice observational cohort, without random allocation.

summary.before: Curesponse, based in Rehovot, Israel, and founded in 2018, is the company whose cResponse test keeps a fragment of a patient's tumour alive, with its blood vessels and immune cells intact, to test which treatments it responds to. The test combines ex vivo tumour-fragment culture with rapid genomics; a 2026 clinical utility study showed the assay can rule out ineffective regimens and reclassify predicted non-responders, and it is distributed in the United Kingdom through EDX Medical. OnCo links it to functional ex vivo drug testing and organoid-guided therapy at scale, to the bottleneck of preclinical models that do not predict people, and to ideas on testing drugs on freshly cut slices of the patient's own tumour. Whether functional testing improves outcomes in a randomised trial is the open question for the whole field. The functional testing page carries the evidence.
summary.after: Curesponse, based in Rehovot, Israel, and founded in 2018, is the company whose cResponse test keeps a fragment of a patient's tumour alive, with its blood vessels and immune cells intact, to test which treatments it responds to. Its methods describe exclusions from a treatment-choice analysis, so this proportion is not by itself a culture-establishment success rate. Reported response agreement and changed physician decisions do not establish improved patient outcomes from using the test. OnCo links it to functional ex vivo drug testing and organoid-guided therapy at scale, to the bottleneck of preclinical models that do not predict people, and to ideas on testing drugs on freshly cut slices of the patient's own tumour. Outcome evidence is specific to the assay and intended use; a randomised result for another functional test does not establish benefit from choosing treatment with cResponse. The functional testing page carries the evidence.

before: Timing and denominators. Hidalgo's 2014 review described four to eight months to a study-ready model; it is a historical review estimate, not a laboratory guarantee. Izumchenko's series reported 578 successful grafts from 1,163 implanted specimens, described as 49 percent, and a mean 16 weeks from engraftment to drug exposure, with substantial variation. That clock is not the whole biopsy-to-decision interval. Keep submitted, established and interpretable donor models separate. Arithmetic check by OnCo: 578 divided by 1,163 is approximately 49.7 percent; the paper itself states 49 percent. Retain the counts and distinguish the reported percentage from this calculation. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4167608/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5834154/

Fidelity is measured, not assumed. Record histology, lineage and relevant molecular features against the source, host strain, site and passage, and species assignment for the mechanism. Ben-David reported mouse-specific copy-number evolution in studied datasets; Woo's direct-DNA analyses reported conservation and showed that measurement method matters. Neither establishes perfect preservation nor inevitable complete divergence for every model. Sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28991255/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7808565/ Engraftment is establishment of growth after implantation; passage transfers an established graft to another host. Reduced growth relative to a control is different from regression below a stated starting burden. Matching molecular features does not validate every drug prediction.

Assay card. Viable material, establishment, passage and animal experiments consume finite material. Report burden or volume with units, baseline and observation clock, exposure and comparator animals, and donor versus animal counts. Failed engraftment and excluded experiments remain visible. Human-specific binding to tumour cells does not establish activity on mouse stromal targets. A graft tested later in a dish has a different experimental setting. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3553601/

A fictional example separates denominators: ten donor specimens are submitted, four establish grafts, three yield an interpretable drug experiment and two meet its response criterion. Establishment is 4/10; response among interpretable donor models is 2/3, not a patient-response rate. A human-specific antibody binding a retained tumour receptor also does not establish binding to mouse-derived vessel targets required by a proposed mechanism.

NCI's model repository uses lineage identity, pathology and human/mouse-content checks and notes that some models evolve with passage. Its procedures and material types are repository-specific. Yang's 2026 primary abstract describes adding patient-derived tumour and mesenchymal cells, human endothelial cells and humanised marrow to a specialised immune-stroma PDX. This is evidence for a defined added-component model, not complete reconstruction of human immunity. Sources: https://dctd.cancer.gov/drug-discovery-development/reagents-materials/pdmr/models ; https://doi.org/10.1007/s00262-026-04349-4

Izumchenko and colleagues compared 129 treatments across 92 people with advanced solid tumours. Their 112/129 agreement figure (87 percent) grouped stable disease with partial and complete responses as positive disease control; reported sensitivity was 96 percent and specificity 70 percent. Requiring the exact RECIST category instead gave 91/129 agreement (71 percent). Responses came from the consulting oncologist and from xenograft volume changes converted to RECIST equivalents. These selected, repeated treatment comparisons are not 129 independent people, a head-to-head accuracy ranking against other model types or a trial showing benefit from assigning treatment by the model.

before.name: Context of use for a tumor model
before.tldr: A model needs the components required to answer its particular question. A model that works for one experiment may leave out the biology needed for another.
before.summary: Tumor models differ in which cancer, stromal and immune components they retain, and those properties can change with the method. A primary organoid study preserved endogenous immune cells and examined checkpoint-blockade responses in that system. This establishes capabilities of a defined model, not a universal ability to predict clinical treatment benefit. The question, retained components, exposure, readout and comparison against relevant observations should accompany a model claim.

notes: Question-first reading framework. Name the intervention, required cells or processes, endpoint, observation time and intended inference. Predicting a molecular change, culture growth, scan response and benefit from a treatment strategy are different questions. Trust belongs to this question and evidence, not the model name or complexity. Include the consequence of an incorrect answer when deciding how much supporting evidence the use needs.

Construction and readout. Record source and identity, retained or added populations, viable window, preparation/version and missing components. Define measured or predicted object, units, reference and uncertainty. Check relevant controls, baseline growth and population attribution. A lower count than a dividing control is not necessarily a count below the start. Reliability within a run, independent biological specimens and correctness answer different questions. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4887336/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30550791/ Human-derived cells or tissue are not complete human physiology. Repeatability can preserve a systematic error; a measured treatment effect does not identify its mechanism without comparisons that distinguish alternative explanations.

Prediction and proposed use. Evaluate outcomes not used to build or tune a rule, retain failures, uncertainty and mismatches, and examine relevant baselines. Attach assay version, population, treatment and endpoint to agreement. Ladan's preoperative breast-slice comparison cannot validate an unrelated postoperative drug or assay. Clinical validity and benefit from using a decision strategy remain distinct; the analytical-versus-clinical-validation owner holds that distinction. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10542784/

Scoped computational analogy. FDA's 2023 device-simulation guidance distinguishes verification of the mathematical implementation from empirical validation with independent observations, and treats calibration as separate from validation. Its stated scope is first-principles computational models in medical-device submissions, not a blanket rule for every machine-learning system or living culture. We use the distinction as a reading framework, not a universal certification ladder. Source: https://www.fda.gov/media/154985/download

Fictional example. A tumour-only culture repeatedly responds to Drug A. This does not test an immune-dependent Drug B or prove benefit because the cells came from a patient. Check the required immune interaction, actual intervention, endpoint and independent validation. Repeatability cannot repair a mismatch between question and model. These are invented drugs and a reading exercise. Complexity is useful when it represents biology necessary for the question and remains measurable. A simpler model may isolate a mechanism, while another model is needed for an interaction absent from it. More components alone do not show better prediction.

Recap. Question, construction, measurement and controls, intended prediction and proposed use are a checklist of distinct questions rather than a mandatory sequence or trust score. State what the model is trusted to answer, the evidence supporting that use and the questions still open.

An original wholly fictional validation exercise uses D0 and its repeated wells only for development, then reserves one pretreatment specimen from each of thirty new donors in an advanced breast-cancer research setting. Lock every fitting, threshold and preprocessing choice before their outcomes. The toy assay counts identified tumour cells after drug A at 0.3 micromoles per litre for 48 hours. Reportability requires malignant identity, calibrated counts, three usable wells per condition, vehicle growth above baseline and the prespecified positive-control response; mechanism results and raw variation remain separate. A treated-count median divided by the vehicle median at or below 0.5 predicts positive, not 50 percent killing. A blinded independent assessor compares the stipulated imaging-volume measurement before treatment and at week six; a decline of at least 20 percent is the invented reference-positive rule, not a clinical response criterion.

The fictional locked rule yields twenty reports and ten no-results among thirty donors. Among reportable cases, six are true positive, three false positive, two false negative and nine true negative, using the exercise's assumed-correct reference labels. There are eight reference positives, twelve negatives, nine positive predictions and eleven negative predictions. Correct classifications are 15/20 (75 percent), sensitivity 6/8 (75 percent), specificity 9/12 (75 percent), and positive predictive value 6/9 (about 66.7 percent). Reportable coverage is 20/30 (about 66.7 percent); 15/30 (50 percent) received a correct reportable classification. The ten no-results keep blank predictions, unknown failure reasons and unspecified outcomes, rather than becoming negative or resistant cases. These truth-based toy metrics do not turn an imperfect real MRI comparator into truth or establish clinical utility.

Preserve the original prediction and version before measuring an independent outcome, compare against the original rule, then investigate agreement, discordance and failures before developing a revision and testing it on new reserved data. A prospective evaluation fixes its predictions before the corresponding outcomes; retrospective analysis examines material and outcomes already observed. Neither label alone establishes useful care. If the toy team changes v1 after inspecting three false positives, v2 is development and v1's matrix and ten no-results remain unchanged. The later breast-study exercise likewise imagines revising a rule after three sensitive dish calls matched intermediate MRI outcomes; those comparisons are not assumed truth labels. Reusing the same twenty cases evaluates fit to the information used for revision. A move from advanced-disease drug A to postoperative drug B changes intended use again, and improvement during several treatments cannot isolate which treatment helped.

There are eight reference positives, twelve negatives, nine positive predictions and eleven negative predictions. Correct classifications are 15/20 (75 percent), sensitivity 6/8 (75 percent), specificity 9/12 (75 percent), and positive predictive value 6/9 (about 66.7 percent). Reportable coverage is 20/30 (about 66.7 percent); 15/30 (50 percent) received a correct reportable classification. The ten no-results keep blank predictions, unknown failure reasons and unspecified outcomes, rather than becoming negative or resistant cases. These truth-based toy metrics do not turn an imperfect real MRI comparator into truth or establish clinical utility.

Preserve the original prediction and version before measuring an independent outcome, compare against the original rule, then investigate agreement, discordance and failures before developing a revision and testing it on new reserved data. A prospective evaluation fixes its predictions before the corresponding outcomes; retrospective analysis examines material and outcomes already observed. Neither label alone establishes useful care. If the toy team changes v1 after inspecting three false positives, v2 is development and v1's matrix and ten no-results remain unchanged. The later breast-study exercise likewise imagines revising a rule after three sensitive dish calls matched intermediate MRI outcomes; those comparisons are not assumed truth labels. Reusing the same twenty cases evaluates fit to the information used for revision. A move from advanced-disease drug A to postoperative drug B changes intended use again, and improvement during several treatments cannot isolate which treatment helped.
